title: Jethro's Visit and the Sharing of Judgment
summary: Jethro, Moses' father-in-law and the priest of Midian, brings Zipporah and her two sons to Moses at the mountain of God. Hearing what the LORD has done, he blesses the LORD, confesses him greater than all other gods, and shares a sacrificial meal with Israel's elders. The next day he watches Moses judge the people alone from morning to evening and advises him to appoint capable, God-fearing men to decide ordinary cases, and Moses does.
story: In chapter 17 one foreign people, Amalek, came out to attack Israel; in chapter 18 another, Midian, comes out to bless. The contrast looks deliberate, and it recalls God's promise to Abraham that those who bless his family would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Moses had fled to Midian as a young man, married Jethro's daughter Zipporah, and was shepherding Jethro's flock when God called him at the bush on Horeb (3:1). Now he is back at the same mountain with the people he was sent to rescue, and the man who once sheltered a fugitive hears the whole story. The chapter also prepares for Sinai. Before God speaks his law in chapter 20, Israel receives a way to administer justice, so the people who will hear the covenant are organized into a community that can keep it.
historical:
The Midianites were a people of the desert fringes, usually placed in northwestern Arabia east of the Gulf of Aqaba, with groups ranging into the Sinai and the Negev. Genesis traces them to Midian, a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2), so like the Amalekites they were distant kin of Israel. Later they appear as enemies, at Peor (Numbers 25 and 31) and in Gideon's day (Judges 6-8), but Moses' in-laws are consistently friendly, and Judges 1:16 says that descendants of Moses' father-in-law, called Kenites, went up with Judah into the land. Some modern scholars have proposed, in what is called the Kenite or Midianite hypothesis, that the worship of the LORD reached Israel through these in-laws; the text presents the reverse, with Jethro learning from Moses what the LORD has done.

The chapter's place in the book is a puzzle. Verse 5 has Israel already camped at the mountain of God, yet the arrival at Sinai is narrated only in 19:1-2, and Deuteronomy 1:9-18 recalls the appointing of judges around the time Israel left Horeb. Ancient Jewish interpreters already debated whether Jethro came before or after the giving of the law. Many commentators think the chapter was placed here by theme, setting the friendly Midianite beside the hostile Amalekite; others read it in sequence, with the courts organized during the long camp at the mountain.
cultural:
Hospitality customs shape the opening scene. Jethro sends word ahead, and Moses goes out to meet him, bows, and kisses him; the Hebrew says they asked each other about their shalom, their peace and welfare, before going into the tent. A father-in-law was owed honor, and Moses gives it in public. The meal in verse 12 is more than hospitality. Eating together after a sacrifice, in the presence of God, was a common way of sealing friendship or alliance, and here the priest of Midian offers the sacrifices while Aaron and the elders of Israel eat with him.

The courtroom scene reflects justice in small societies, where disputes were brought to a respected leader who heard both sides in public and gave a ruling. Moses holds two roles at once: he decides cases, and he makes known the statutes and instructions of God, since in Israel law came from God rather than from a king. Jethro's units of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens are military divisions, and the word for their leaders (sar) usually means an officer. The qualifications he names are moral before they are practical: men who fear God, who can be trusted, and who hate dishonest gain. The same concern returns in the law of 23:8: “Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous.”
literary: The chapter has two halves of nearly equal length, each built around a day. On the first day Jethro hears, rejoices, confesses, and worships; on the next he watches, questions, advises, and goes home. Both halves turn on the word good. Jethro rejoices over all the good the LORD has done for Israel (verse 9), then tells Moses that what he is doing “is not good” (verse 17), an echo of God's verdict on the man alone in Genesis 2:18. Hearing frames the whole: Jethro heard at the start (verse 1), and Moses listened to his father-in-law at the end (verse 24). The names of the two sons retell Moses' life in miniature: Gershom for the foreigner in a foreign land, and Eliezer for the man whose father's God delivered him from Pharaoh's sword.

outline.t: Jethro brings Zipporah and her sons to the mountain of God
Moses tells the story; Jethro blesses the LORD and offers sacrifice
Moses judges the people alone from morning to evening
Jethro's counsel: share the load with capable men
Moses appoints judges, and Jethro goes home

doctrines.note: A Midianite priest hears what God has done, blesses the LORD, and says, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods” (verse 11). The plagues were sent so that the nations would know the LORD, and here one foreigner does. The exodus was never meant to be news for Israel alone.

Good counsel comes to Moses from outside Israel, and he takes it. The text treats Jethro's plan as wise without claiming it was revealed from heaven, and Jethro himself makes it conditional on God's direction (verse 23). Wisdom includes the humble skill of ordering work so that people are not crushed by it.

Justice in Israel is God's before it is anyone else's; Moses brings the people's causes to God and teaches his statutes. Those who share the work must fear God, be trustworthy, and refuse bribes, because a judge who can be bought misrepresents the God whose justice he administers.

words.note: Choten, a relative by marriage, usually a wife's father. It appears thirteen times in this chapter, far more often than Jethro's name, keeping the relationship in view: this is family. The same consonants, with different vowels, spell chatan, son-in-law or bridegroom, which bears on the question of Hobab in Judges 4:11 (see the hard question).

Shaphat, to judge. The Hebrew word is broader than handing down a verdict; it means to put things right, to govern, and to settle disputes, which is why the leaders in the book of Judges are called by a word from the same root. Jethro's plan shares the work of judging, but the standard stays God's.

Torah, instruction or law. Before the Ten Commandments are given, Moses is already making known the statutes and instructions of God (verse 16). The word is usually connected with teaching and pointing out the way, and its range is wider than rules: it is guidance for how to live. It later becomes the name of the first five books of the Bible.

christ: The link between this chapter and Christ is thematic rather than predictive. Jethro belongs to a line of foreigners in the Old Testament who hear what the God of Israel has done and turn to him, with Rahab, Ruth, and Naaman, and they anticipate the gospel going out to the nations. The Magi who come from the east to worship the child Jesus (Matthew 2) stand in the same line. The chapter also shows a mediator who cannot carry the whole people alone. The concern returns in Numbers 11, where God puts his Spirit on seventy elders, and again in Acts 6, where the apostles have the church choose seven men so that they can give themselves “to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4). Hebrews presents the one mediator who needs no relief: Christ “always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

hard.q: Is Moses' father-in-law named Jethro, Reuel, or Hobab?
hard.a: He is Jethro here and in chapters 3-4, but Reuel in 2:18. Numbers 10:29 speaks of Hobab, son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses' father-in-law, while Judges 4:11 calls Hobab himself the father-in-law of Moses. Several explanations are offered. Some suggest that Reuel was the head of the clan, perhaps Zipporah's grandfather, so that the girls in 2:18 return to the family patriarch, while Jethro was the father-in-law and Hobab his son. Others note that people in the ancient Near East often bore more than one name, and that Jethro may have been a second name or title. Because the Hebrew words for father-in-law and son-in-law share the same consonants, some read Hobab in Judges 4:11 as Moses' brother-in-law, as several English versions do. Many critical scholars see the variation as a trace of different traditions woven into the Pentateuch. The difficulty is real but narrow. Every account agrees that Moses married into a Midianite priestly family that treated him and Israel with kindness.

questions: Jethro rejoiced over what God had done for someone else's people. What would it look like to rejoice in God's work among people who are not your own group?
Moses heard hard advice from his father-in-law and acted on it. What makes it difficult to receive correction about the way we work, especially in something we believe God gave us to do?
Jethro's judges had to fear God, be trustworthy, and hate dishonest gain. Why do character qualifications come before skill in the leaders Scripture describes?
